title: J.A. Bayona and Oscar-Winning Producers Join The Dragon Letter
excerpt:
Student Academy Award winner The Dragon Letter gains three prominent executive producers.
Its Ladakhi director is also developing a feature-length adaptation of the story.
body_md:
The Dragon Letter, a short film recognized at the Student Academy Awards, has attracted three prominent executive producers as its director develops a feature-length version. Spanish filmmaker J.A. Bayona, Oscar-winning producer Guneet Monga Kapoor and chef-filmmaker Vikas Khanna have joined the project, giving a personal story from Ladakh a wider international network of supporters.

Directed by Stanzin Jigmet, the film received the narrative Gold award at the 53rd Student Academy Awards and has been submitted for consideration in the live-action short category at the 99th Academy Awards. Submission is not the same as an Oscar nomination. ESCAC Films in Spain produced the short in association with India's Sikhya Entertainment, with production taking place in Ladakh and Barcelona.

The story follows Skarma, a ten-year-old boy asked to write a letter to his sponsor in Barcelona. Every child in his class is expected to reproduce the same words and draw the same dragon, but Skarma wants to express something of his own. His struggle to find the courage to do so becomes the film's emotional center.

Jigmet drew the premise from his own experiences at a Himalayan boarding school. Friends with European sponsors were required to send annual thank-you letters, and he remembers decorating some of those letters with dragon drawings. These small acts of childhood assistance and friendship became the basis for a story about individuality and kindness.

Bayona, whose credits include The Orphanage, The Impossible and Society of the Snow, has highlighted the film's ability to connect a very specific Himalayan setting with universal emotions. Monga Kapoor, who won an Academy Award for The Elephant Whisperers, similarly points to the lasting importance of seemingly minor gestures of support between children.

The production history is nearly as compelling as the story. Jigmet grew up in a village without a cinema and initially learned filmmaking through YouTube. He later received an opportunity to study directing at ESCAC in Barcelona. In Ladakh, he worked with nonprofessional performers, a small crew and a school full of children, some of whom helped with lighting equipment. The Barcelona unit offered a contrasting experience with professional actors and a larger production team.

Khanna, known for MasterChef India and his film The Last Color, has also praised the way the short depicts children's care for one another. Together, the executive producers bring experience across international filmmaking, awards campaigns and cultural storytelling. Their involvement could broaden the film's reach, although it does not guarantee any particular award result.

Jigmet is currently focused on the short film's awards campaign while developing a longer adaptation. No confirmed production start or release date for that feature has been announced. For now, the project demonstrates how an intimate memory from a remote community can become the foundation for an internationally supported film.
